::: {.visual-explainer .explainer-repair}


Fine-tuning [Goodfire's four-layer, 67-million-parameter language model](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters) to predict German less accurately also worsens its Dutch predictions.
The repair must restore Dutch prediction quality while preserving the intended German change.

A compact repair can undo much of this damage. If a new fine-tune causes similar damage, can we reuse that repair?
I test this on two fine-tunes trained independently from the same base model, with the same recipe on different
samples from the same data distribution.

## The same starting repair, two ways to reuse it

The earlier fine-tune is the **donor** and its correction is the **donor repair**. Each repair adds a rank-one update,
formed from an input and an output vector, to each of 24 weight matrices; all other weights stay fixed. The repairs
operate directly on the weight matrices, independently of Goodfire's parameter decomposition.

To test whether the donor's directions suffice for the new damage, I keep its input and output vectors fixed
and fit 24 scalar coefficients. I compare this with donor initialization: starting from the same repair and
training both vectors.

Fresh fitting learns both vectors from a new initialization. Comparing it with donor initialization tests
whether the earlier repair provides a useful starting point. All three have the same rank, objective and norm limit,
but different numbers of fitted parameters: 24 for scalar fitting and 55,296 for donor-initialized or fresh fitting.

The repair is trained to match the base model's predictions on Dutch and the fine-tuned model's predictions on
German, English, French, Spanish and Italian. [Selection](index.qmd#sec-app-methods) constrains German drift and
limits increases in prediction loss on the other preserved languages.

## Keeping the directions leaves damage behind

Recovery is the fraction of the fine-tune's extra Dutch prediction loss removed by a repair.
At the full budget, fitting scalar coefficients only recovers about **87%** of the Dutch damage on the first target and **78%** on the second.
Donor initialization, which lets the directions change, raises recovery to about **98–99%**.
All full-budget repairs shown preserved the German effect and met the constraints on the other languages.

Fitting budgets exclude a separate selection and diagnostic pool of **57,344 prediction positions**, shared by all
families. The two methods that reuse the donor repair assume it already exists; its [one-time cost](index.qmd#sec-app-cost)
is separate.

```{=html}
<figure class="explainer-figure" aria-labelledby="repair-full-caption">
  <div id="repair-full-chart" class="explainer-chart"></div>
  <figcaption id="repair-full-caption">Full budget: 2,048 fit tokens and checkpoint selection from runs of up to 600 steps.
  Fit tokens count prediction positions, excluding the initial context token of each window.
  0% means no repair; 100% restores the base model's Dutch prediction loss. Whiskers show 95% bootstrap intervals
  over 92 Europarl readout dates for each fixed target; variation across new fine-tunes or donors remains unmeasured.</figcaption>
</figure>
<p id="repair-primary-result" class="explainer-finding">Donor initialization exceeds the scalar-coefficient fit by 11.3 percentage
points on the first target and 20.4 points on the second.</p>
```

<details class="visual-details">
<summary>How the scalar coefficients were fitted</summary>

The gap could reflect incomplete scalar fitting. To check this, two additional runs optimize the same full-batch
loss to convergence from different starts. Selection includes those candidates and ordinary training checkpoints.
The shortfall survives this expanded search; other choices of coefficients remain untested.

</details>

## The donor helps most when fitting is constrained

Allowing the directions to change improves recovery, but fresh fitting also recovers most of the damage. I compare donor
initialization with fresh fitting to see what the donor contributes as a starting point.

At the full budget, donor initialization leads the first fresh seed by **1.1–1.4 percentage points**. Both
confidence intervals are above zero but inside the study's chosen **±2 percentage-point tolerance** for treating
performance as practically equivalent. The lead is comparable to differences between two fresh seeds.

To see whether the donor helps more when fitting is constrained, I vary both the fit-token budget and the step cap.
At 256 fit tokens and 50 steps, the lead is about **4 percentage points**; only one fresh seed was tested at that budget.
